subtype: Approach: venting in the group chat [Pitfall]
passage: Honestly, Jagdish, the group chat post was the worst idea I had all year. My best friend Minal had promised to sit with me at the quiz and then sat with the debate girls. I was furious. So I typed, "Some people say they're your friend and then disappear." No name. Just that, in the class chat. For about ten minutes it was lovely: hearts, "who is it??", someone writing "been there." Then Minal read it. Everyone knew who, because of the quiz. She left the chat and did not pick up my call. Now when I want to say sorry and explain, I can't even begin, because she thinks the whole class was laughing at her. I wanted one person to hear me, and I told forty. I'm Sharmila, and I would delete that post if I could.

qa.q: Where did Sharmila post the vague complaint?
qa.a: Sharmila posted it in the class chat.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when typing the post, and what set it off?
qa.a: Sharmila was hurt and furious because Minal promised to sit at the quiz and then sat with the debate girls.

qa.q: What could Sharmila do instead to be heard by Minal, and why?
qa.a: Sharmila could ask Minal for a private one-to-one talk and say how the quiz felt, because an honest talk needs to feel safe rather than public.

qa.q: How does the post look to Minal?
qa.a: Minal, named by everyone's guess, likely feels embarrassed and rejected, which is why Minal left the chat and ignored the call.

grounding: Hurt and angry, the student posts vague complaints in a shared chat, which brings brief sympathy but spreads the conflict, embarrasses the friend and makes an honest talk harder.

subtype: Approach: venting in the group chat [Pitfall]
passage: I'm in the class group chat, so I saw it happen on Sunday night. Rekha posted: "Some people can't keep anything to themselves. Good to know who your real friends are." No names. Within minutes there were twelve replies. "Who??" "Hugs, Rekha." "Is it about you-know-who?" Everyone guessed Trisha, because the two of them had been inseparable until Friday. Trisha didn't reply at all. On Monday she sat at the back, eyes on her desk, and two girls whispered when she walked past. I don't know what Trisha did, or exactly what Rekha was feeling. Rekha looked pleased on Sunday night and miserable by Monday lunch. When Trisha finally walked up to her in the corridor, Rekha turned away. I think the chat had made it too big to talk about.

qa.q: How many replies came within minutes of Rekha's post?
How did Rekha's mood seem to change from Sunday night to Monday?
qa.a: She seemed pleased by the sympathy on Sunday night but miserable by Monday lunch, once the conflict had spread.

qa.q: What could Rekha have done instead of posting?
qa.a: Messaged Trisha privately or asked to talk, so the hurt could be sorted out between the two of them without an audience.

qa.q: What is Monday like for Trisha?
qa.a: Trisha seems embarrassed and isolated, sitting at the back with eyes on the desk while others whisper.

grounding: An observer watches a student's vague post in the class chat draw sympathy, spread the conflict and make a real talk harder.

subtype: Approach: venting in the group chat [Pitfall]
passage:
Friday. Jyoti skips Varun's cricket match to go to the mall with the new kids, after promising to come. Varun waits by the boundary, checking the gate every over.
Saturday. At midnight Varun types into the class group: "Funny how some people only show up when it suits them." Hearts and "bro who??" pour in. For an hour he feels better. Then Jyoti's cousin replies, "If this is about Jyoti, just say it." Screenshots start going round.
Monday. Jyoti won't look at him in the corridor. At lunch, when Varun finally says, "Can we talk?", Jyoti says, "Why? You already told everyone," and walks off. Varun realises he never actually told Jyoti what hurt.

qa.q: What did Varun type into the class group?
qa.a: Funny how some people only show up when it suits them.

qa.q: How did Varun feel after posting?
qa.a: He felt better for an hour, comforted by the replies, but the relief faded once screenshots began going round.
Apologise to Jyoti for posting in public, then say privately what hurt about the missed match.

qa.q: Why might Jyoti refuse to talk on Monday?
qa.a: Jyoti feels publicly shamed by the post and the screenshots, so a private talk now feels pointless.

grounding: Shows over three days how venting in a group chat brings brief sympathy, then spreads the conflict and blocks an honest talk.
